title: Docker
description: Containers, images, Dockerfiles, and Compose for reproducible environments.
blurb: Containers, images, Dockerfiles, and Compose for reproducible environments.
careerApplications: 'It works on my machine' is a real, common failure mode Docker exists to eliminate — expected baseline knowledge for most SWE roles.

beginner: Basic docker CLI (run, ps, stop, logs)

lessons.title: Why containers exist
objectives: State the problem containers solve
Distinguish a container from a VM

lessons.explanation: 'It works on my machine' happens because your machine has different OS versions, library versions, and config than the server. A container packages your app WITH its exact dependencies into one portable unit that runs identically anywhere Docker is installed.
examples:
# Without Docker: 'runs fine locally, breaks in prod'
# because prod has Python 3.9 and your machine has 3.12

# With Docker: the container HAS Python 3.9 baked in,
# identical everywhere
commonMistakes: Thinking a container IS a lightweight VM — it isn't; it shares the host kernel, which is exactly why it's fast but also why it isn't as isolated as a real VM.

lessons.title: Images vs containers
objectives: Define image and container precisely
Explain the relationship between them
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: container registry.
lessons.explanation: An image is a read-only template — your app plus its dependencies, frozen as a set of layered files. A container is a running instance of that image, with its own writable layer on top.
examples:
docker images        # list images (the templates)
docker ps             # list running containers (instances)
docker run python:3.11  # spins up a NEW container from the python:3.11 image
commonMistakes: Confusing 'stopping a container' with 'deleting the image' — stopping just pauses the running instance; the image (template) is untouched.
lessons.careerRelevance: This class/object mental model is exactly how you'll reason about containers day to day. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Basic docker CLI
objectives: Run, list, stop, and inspect containers from the command line
Explain how docker run changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect docker run with docker ps and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A small set of commands covers most day-to-day container use: `docker run` starts a new container from an image, `docker ps` lists running containers, `docker stop` gracefully stops one, and `docker logs` shows its output — essential for debugging.
examples:
docker run -d --name myapp -p 8000:8000 myimage
docker ps
docker logs myapp
docker stop myapp
commonMistakes: Forgetting `-p` (port mapping) and then wondering why the app 'isn't responding' — the container is running, but nothing outside it can reach the port.
lessons.careerRelevance: You'll run these commands dozens of times a day once containers are part of your workflow.

lessons.title: Writing a Dockerfile
objectives: Write a Dockerfile that builds a working image
Explain each common instruction
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: HEALTHCHECK.
lessons.explanation: A Dockerfile is a recipe for building an image: FROM picks a base image, COPY brings in your code, RUN executes setup commands (like installing dependencies) at build time, and CMD specifies what runs when the container starts.
examples:
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
commonMistakes: Copying all your code BEFORE installing dependencies — this busts the build cache on every code change, since Docker rebuilds every layer after the first one that changed.
lessons.careerRelevance: Writing a correct, efficient Dockerfile is a common practical task in backend/SWE interviews and onboarding. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: A Dockerfile is a recipe for building an image: FROM picks a base image, COPY brings in your code, RUN executes setup commands (like installing dependencies) at build time, and CMD specifies what runs when the container starts.

lessons.title: Volumes & persisting data
objectives: Explain why container data is ephemeral by default
Use a volume to persist data
Explain how volume changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect volume with ephemeral storage and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed — anything your app wrote (a database file, uploaded images) is gone too, unless you use a volume: a directory managed by Docker (or mounted from the host) that survives container restarts and removal.
examples:
docker run -v mydata:/app/data myimage
# 'mydata' volume persists even if the container is deleted and recreated
commonMistakes: Storing a database's data files inside the container with no volume — a routine `docker rm` silently wipes the database.
lessons.careerRelevance: Any containerized service with real data (a database, file uploads) needs volumes to be production-safe.

lessons.title: Docker Compose for multi-container apps
objectives: Read and write a docker-compose.yml for a multi-service app
Explain how docker-compose.yml changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect docker-compose.yml with services and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Real apps are rarely one container — a web app + a database + a cache is typical. Docker Compose lets you define all of them, plus how they connect, in one YAML file, and bring the whole stack up or down with a single command.
examples:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on: [db]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
commonMistakes: Assuming `depends_on` waits for the database to be READY (accepting connections) — it only waits for the container to START, which is not the same thing; apps often need their own retry.
lessons.careerRelevance: Local development environments for most real projects are defined with Compose.
lessons.explain: Real apps are rarely one container — a web app + a database + a cache is typical. Docker Compose lets you define all of them, plus how they connect, in one YAML file, and bring the whole stack up or down with a single command.

lessons.title: Multi-Stage Builds & Image Optimization
objectives: Use multi-stage builds to keep production images small and free of build-time dependencies
Explain how multi-stage build changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect multi-stage build with build stage and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A naive Dockerfile often ships the whole build toolchain (compilers, dev dependencies, source maps) inside the final image, even though none of that is needed to actually RUN the app -- this bloats image size and increases attack surface.
examples:
# Stage 1: build
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: run -- only the compiled output ships, not node_modules or source
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
commonMistakes: Shipping the entire build stage (compilers, dev dependencies, source files) in the final image because it's simpler than setting up a second stage -- this can make images several times.
lessons.careerRelevance: Multi-stage builds are the standard, expected way to keep production images lean in any real containerized deployment -- an interviewer will notice if a candidate ships an unoptimized image without knowing why it matters.
lessons.explain: A naive Dockerfile often ships the whole build toolchain (compilers, dev dependencies, source maps) inside the final image, even though none of that is needed to actually RUN the app -- this bloats image size and increases attack surface.
lessons.example:
# Stage 1: build
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json .
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: run -- only the compiled output ships, not node_modules or source

WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist

lessons.title: Container Networking & Environment Configuration
objectives: Configure containers with environment variables and understand how containers reach each other over Docker's network
Explain how environment variable changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect environment variable with env-file and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Environment variables (passed via `docker run -e KEY=value` or an `--env-file`, or the `environment:` section in Compose) let the same image behave differently across environments -- a database URL, an API key, a feature flag -- without baking those values into the image itself, which also keeps secrets out of version control.
examples:
docker run -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/app -e DEBUG=false my-app

# in docker-compose.yml, a Flask service reaching a Redis service:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    environment:
      - REDIS_HOST=redis   # service name, NOT localhost
  redis:
    image: redis:7
commonMistakes: Using `localhost` to reach another container -- from inside a container, localhost refers to that container itself, not the host machine or a sibling service; use the other service's name on.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly configuring environment variables and inter-container networking is what separates a container that works on one machine from a deployable, environment-agnostic service.
lessons.explain: Environment variables (passed via `docker run -e KEY=value` or an `--env-file`, or the `environment:` section in Compose) let the same image behave differently across environments -- a database URL, an API key, a feature flag -- without baking those values into the image itself, which also keeps secrets out of version control.

interviewPreparation.q: Why would you use a multi-stage build instead of a single-stage Dockerfile?
interviewPreparation.a: A single-stage build often ships build tools, dev dependencies, and source files that aren't needed to run the app, bloating the image and increasing attack surface. A multi-stage build compiles or installs in an early stage, then copies only the finished artifacts into a fresh, minimal final stage -- meaningfully smaller and cleaner images.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does a container exit immediately if its main process finishes, unlike a virtual machine?
interviewPreparation.a: A container's lifecycle is tied directly to its main process (the CMD/ENTRYPOINT) -- there's no separate 'OS' running underneath that keeps going. A VM keeps running its guest OS regardless of any single process; a container IS essentially that one process, so when it exits, the container exits with it.

interviewPreparation.q: How do two containers in the same Docker Compose project actually reach each other?
interviewPreparation.a: By service name, over the shared bridge network Compose creates automatically -- not by localhost or a hardcoded IP. A web service reaches a database service at `db:5432`, for example, because Compose's internal DNS resolves service names to the right container.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you handle configuration (like a database URL or API key) that differs between dev, staging, and production?
interviewPreparation.a: Environment variables, injected at run time (via `-e`, an env file, or Compose's environment section) rather than baked into the image -- the same image should work across environments, with only its configuration changing, and secrets specifically should never be committed into the image or version control.

interviewPreparation.q: A container works fine on your machine but fails in a teammate's environment. What would you check?
interviewPreparation.a: Whether the failure is actually environment-specific config (missing env vars, a different port already in use) versus something baked into the image that assumed your local setup -- `docker logs` and comparing exact environment variables between the two setups usually narrows it down quickly.

capstone.title: Package and deploy your Backend + API system with Docker
capstone.description: Take the backend service and API you already built (from the Backend and APIs capstones, or equivalents) and make them genuinely deployable: multi-stage Dockerfiles that keep images lean, a Compose setup that wires the service to its real dependencies (a database, a cache), environment-based configuration instead of hardcoded values, and a documented account of at least one real container failure you hit and how you debugged it. This capstone isn't about building new backend logic -- it's about proving you can package and run what you already built reliably.
deliverables: A multi-stage Dockerfile for the service, with a documented before/after image size comparison
A docker-compose.yml wiring the service to at least one real dependency (database and/or cache) via service-name networking, not hardcoded IPs
Configuration driven by environment variables (e.g. database URL, debug flag) -- nothing environment-specific hardcoded into the image
A short written account of one real container failure you hit while building this (a crash, a networking issue, a build cache problem) and exactly how you diagnosed and fixed it
Volumes correctly used for anything that needs to persist across container restarts (e.g. database data)
capstone.portfolioTips: The image-size comparison and the real debugging story are the two things that make this capstone distinct from 'I wrote a Dockerfile' -- they're concrete, specific evidence that you understand why multi-stage builds and container lifecycle matter, not just the syntax.

industryUsage.usage: Containerization itself originated here, and multi-stage builds specifically were introduced to solve the exact 'bloated production image' problem this course covers.
Runs its backend microservices in containers, with image size and startup time directly affecting deployment speed and infrastructure cost at its scale.
Containerizes services as a baseline expectation before they ever reach Kubernetes -- Docker fluency (Dockerfiles, Compose for local dev) is assumed groundwork for the orchestration layer on top.
